body:
Conservation involves more than protecting individual animals

A forest is not merely a collection of trees. It is an ecosystem in which plants, animals, microorganisms, soil, water and climate interact. Trees provide shelter and food, insects pollinate plants, predators regulate animal populations, and forest vegetation helps protect soil and water resources.

When forest land is cleared, the damage may extend beyond the loss of trees. Wildlife habitats can become fragmented, animal movement may be obstructed, and local communities may lose access to resources on which they depend.

Biodiversity is the variety of life at the genetic, species and ecosystem levels. Conserving biodiversity therefore requires protection of species, habitats and ecological relationships. It also requires rules for the sustainable use of biological resources.

Different laws address different problems

India uses several complementary legal instruments because protecting a species, regulating forest land and recognising community rights are different governmental functions.

Law or policyPrincipal concernCentral idea
Indian Forest Act, 1927Forest administrationClassification, management and regulation of forests and forest produce
Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972Wildlife and habitatsProtection of specified species and legally declared protected areas
Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam, 1980Forest land diversionPrior Central Government approval for specified changes in forest land use
National Forest Policy, 1988Forest policy objectivesEcological stability, tree cover, conservation and people's participation
Forest Rights Act, 2006Forest-dependent communitiesRecognition of eligible individual and community forest rights
Biological Diversity Act, 2002Biological resources and traditional knowledgeConservation, sustainable use and equitable benefit sharing

The titles of these laws contain their original years. Later amendments have changed important provisions. For example, the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980 received its present name in 2023, but it remains the law originally enacted in 1980.

In-situ and ex-situ conservation

In-situ conservation protects organisms within their natural habitats. National parks, wildlife sanctuaries and other protected areas are major examples. Conserving an entire habitat also protects ecological interactions among species.

Ex-situ conservation protects organisms outside their natural habitats. Zoological parks, botanical gardens and seed banks are examples. These measures may help threatened species, but they do not replace the need to conserve functioning natural ecosystems.

The distinction matters because the Wild Life (Protection) Act concentrates heavily on species and habitats, while biological diversity law also governs how biological resources and associated knowledge are accessed and used.

Prelims focus

  • The Wild Life (Protection) Act was enacted in 1972.
  • The forest diversion law was enacted in 1980 and renamed in 2023.
  • The National Forest Policy was adopted in 1988.
  • The Biological Diversity Act is titled the Biological Diversity Act, 2002.
  • The Forest Rights Act is titled the Forest Rights Act, 2006.
  • Trap: Protecting wildlife, granting forest diversion approval and recognising forest rights are not the same legal function.

[NCERT, Science, Class 8, Chapter 7, Conservation of Plants and Animals, printed pp. 77–85; NCERT, Biology, Class 12, Chapter 15, Biodiversity and Conservation, sections 15.1 and 15.2; National Biodiversity Authority, Frequently Asked Questions, questions 2, 8 and 9, consulted 1 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Conserving a forest means protecting its wildlife, habitat and relationship with nearby communities.

pictures.alt: A connected forest allows wildlife movement; clearing divides it into isolated patches and interrupts movement even though trees remain.
pictures.caption: Habitat fragmentation affects wildlife even where some forest patches remain.

title: Why India Has Separate Laws for Wildlife, Forests and Biodiversity

body:
Purpose and scope of the Act

The Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972 is India's principal central legislation for protecting wild animals, specified plants and their habitats. It regulates hunting, possession and trade in wildlife, establishes protected-area categories and creates wildlife conservation institutions.

Wildlife protection is not restricted to national parks and sanctuaries. A species protected under the Act remains subject to the relevant legal protection even when it occurs outside a protected area.

Hunting is generally prohibited

Section 9 prohibits hunting wild animals listed in Schedules I and II, except where the Act specifically permits it. Hunting includes activities such as killing, capturing or attempting to capture protected wild animals within the statutory definition.

The prohibition is not completely without exceptions. Section 11 permits specified action in limited circumstances, including action concerning animals dangerous to human life or animals disabled or diseased beyond recovery, under a reasoned written order of the Chief Wild Life Warden, or an authorised officer for Schedule II animals; a Schedule I animal may be ordered killed only if it cannot be captured, tranquilised or translocated. Section 12 allows the Chief Wild Life Warden to issue reasoned written hunting permits for special purposes, such as education and scientific research, with prior Central Government permission for Schedule I animals and prior State Government permission for other wild animals.

An animal entering agricultural land does not automatically become available for unrestricted hunting. The applicable schedule, lawful authorisation and statutory conditions must be considered.

The four schedules after the 2022 amendment

The Wild Life (Protection) Amendment Act, 2022 came into force on 1 April 2023. A major change was the reduction of the earlier 6 schedules to 4 schedules.

ScheduleSubjectPrincipal distinction
Schedule ISpecified wild animalsHigher level of statutory protection and stricter penalties for relevant offences
Schedule IIOther specified wild animalsProtected animals subject to the Act's regulatory provisions
Schedule IIISpecified plantsRestrictions on picking, uprooting, cultivation and trade, subject to the Act
Schedule IVCITES-listed specimensRegulation of international trade in listed species and specimens

Blackbuck, a well-known species associated with Gujarat's grasslands, is listed in Schedule I. The law protects specified plants as well as animals; it is incorrect to assume that wildlife legislation deals only with mammals and birds.

What happened to the former vermin schedule?

The former Schedule V for vermin was removed during the restructuring. However, Section 62 still allows the Central Government to notify specified Schedule II wild animals as vermin for a particular area and period. During the notification's operation, the animal is deemed not to be included in Schedule II for the specified area and period.

Thus, removing the old Schedule V did not eliminate the Central Government's limited power to make area-specific and time-specific vermin notifications.

International trade and invasive alien species

CITES stands for the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora. It regulates international trade in listed species so that such trade does not threaten their survival.

The 2022 amendment introduced provisions for CITES implementation, including a Management Authority and Scientific Authority. The Management Authority issues trade permits and certificates; the Scientific Authority advises whether trade would be detrimental to the survival of the species.

The amendment also introduced Section 62A, empowering the Central Government to regulate or prohibit the import, trade, possession or proliferation of notified invasive alien species that threaten Indian wildlife or habitats.

An IUCN Red List category is a scientific assessment of extinction risk. A Wild Life (Protection) Act schedule is a legal listing. A CITES listing concerns international trade controls. These classifications serve different purposes and must not be treated as interchangeable.

Prelims focus

  • Section 9 deals with the general prohibition of hunting scheduled wild animals.
  • Sections 11 and 12 provide limited statutory exceptions and permits.
  • The 2022 amendment took effect on 1 April 2023.
  • The amended Act has 4 schedules: 2 for protected wild animals, 1 for specified plants and 1 for CITES-listed specimens.
  • Section 62 permits specified, temporary vermin notifications for Schedule II animals.
  • Trap: Schedule IV is not another general category of domestically protected animals; it addresses CITES-listed specimens.

[The Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972, India Code consolidated text updated 1 April 2023, sections 9, 11, 12, 17A–17D, 49D–49R, 62 and 62A, and Schedules I–IV; Wild Life (Protection) Amendment Act, 2022, Act 18 of 2022; commencement notification S.O. 1394(E), 22 March 2023. Official legal texts consulted 1 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Schedules I and II protect animals, III covers specified plants, and IV covers CITES-listed specimens; the amendment reduced schedules from 6 to 4.
pictures.caption: Remember the subject of each schedule, not merely its number.

title: Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972: Species Protection and the Four Schedules

body:
Why protected areas are created

Protecting a species without protecting its habitat is often insufficient. Animals need places to feed, breed, shelter and move. Protected areas provide legal safeguards for ecologically important landscapes and the species living within them.

Under the Wild Life (Protection) Act, the principal protected-area categories are wildlife sanctuaries, national parks, conservation reserves and community reserves. Their legal conditions are not identical.

Wildlife sanctuaries and national parks

A wildlife sanctuary is declared under Sections 18 and 26A. It protects wildlife and habitat while regulating entry, resource use and other activities. The Collector inquires into existing rights and may exclude land, acquire or accept surrender of rights, or allow their continuation in consultation with the Chief Wild Life Warden. Some lawful rights and activities may continue subject to restrictions, permits and applicable forest-rights protections.

A national park is declared under Section 35. It normally provides a stricter regime for habitat protection. Claims must be settled and all rights over the included land must vest in the State Government before final notification; livestock grazing is prohibited, and livestock may enter only when used as a vehicle by a person authorised to enter the park.

Neither category permits unrestricted hunting, habitat destruction or resource extraction.

FeatureWildlife sanctuaryNational park
Principal provisionSections 18 and 26ASection 35
PurposeWildlife and habitat protectionStrong protection of wildlife and ecosystems
Existing rightsConsidered and regulated under lawClaims settled; land rights vested in the State Government
Livestock grazingMay be regulated where lawfully permittedProhibited

Conservation reserves and community reserves

A conservation reserve, under Section 36A, may be declared by the State Government on government-owned land, especially land adjoining national parks or sanctuaries or land connecting protected areas. The State Government consults local communities before declaring such an area. This category is particularly useful for habitat connectivity.

A community reserve, under Section 36C, may be declared where a community or individual voluntarily undertakes conservation on private or community land outside an existing national park, sanctuary or conservation reserve. Changes in land use require the prescribed management committee resolution and State Government approval.

The key distinction is land and participation: a conservation reserve generally concerns government-owned land, while a community reserve concerns voluntarily conserved private or community land.

Tiger reserves and biosphere reserves

A tiger reserve is notified under the tiger conservation provisions of the Wild Life (Protection) Act, especially Section 38V, under which the State Government notifies the reserve on the recommendation of the National Tiger Conservation Authority. Its management involves a core or critical tiger habitat and a surrounding buffer or peripheral area, with the core intended to remain inviolate for tiger conservation and the buffer promoting coexistence between wildlife and human activity, with due recognition of forest dwellers' rights.

Project Tiger began in 1973 as a conservation programme. A tiger reserve is a legally notified conservation area, while Project Tiger is the programme under which tiger conservation has been pursued. The two expressions are related but do not mean exactly the same thing.

A biosphere reserve is a broader conservation and sustainable-use designation that seeks to combine biodiversity protection, research and compatible human activities. It is not itself one of the four protected-area categories created by the Wild Life (Protection) Act. A biosphere reserve may contain national parks or sanctuaries within it.

Recognisable examples from Gujarat

Gujarat provides several useful examples of in-situ conservation:

  • Gir National Park and Wildlife Sanctuary protect important habitat of the Asiatic lion.
  • Velavadar Blackbuck National Park protects grassland habitat associated with blackbuck and other grassland wildlife.
  • Marine National Park, Gulf of Kachchh protects marine and coastal habitats, demonstrating that national parks need not consist of terrestrial forests.

The examples show that protected areas can conserve forests, grasslands, wetlands and marine ecosystems. Their protection depends on the legal notification and applicable rules, not on whether an area visually resembles a dense forest.

Prelims focus

  • Wildlife sanctuary: Sections 18 and 26A.
  • National park: Section 35.
  • Conservation reserve: Section 36A.
  • Community reserve: Section 36C.
  • Tiger reserve: Section 38V; Project Tiger began in 1973.
  • Trap: A biosphere reserve does not automatically become a national park, and a national park need not be a forested area.

[The Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972, India Code, sections 18–36D and 38V; NCERT, Science, Class 8, Chapter 7, sections 7.3–7.8, printed pp. 78–83; NCERT, Biology, Class 12, Chapter 15, section 15.2.2; Wildlife Institute of India, Gujarat protected-area directory, consulted 1 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: The Act defines protected-area categories and tiger reserves with core and buffer; a broader biosphere reserve may contain parks or sanctuaries.
pictures.caption: Different protected-area designations address different conservation needs.

pictures.alt: A conservation worker observes shorebirds beside tidal pools and mangroves in the Gulf of Kachchh, with a distant fisher and boat.
pictures.caption: Marine conservation in the Gulf of Kachchh protects coastal habitats and their wildlife.

title: India's Protected Areas: National Parks, Sanctuaries and Community Conservation

body:
Conservation requires institutions at several levels

A conservation law establishes duties and powers, but institutions must implement them. In India, some bodies provide policy guidance, some manage protected areas, some regulate zoos, and others address wildlife crime or species-specific conservation.

National and State Boards for Wild Life

The National Board for Wild Life (NBWL) is constituted under Section 5A of the Wild Life (Protection) Act. It is chaired by the Prime Minister. It advises on wildlife conservation and protection and performs functions assigned by the Act. Its Standing Committee carries out important functions relating to proposals affecting wildlife habitats under the applicable framework.

The State Board for Wild Life (SBWL) is constituted under Section 6 and is chaired by the Chief Minister. It advises the State Government on wildlife protection, protected areas and related conservation measures.

These boards are not substitutes for field authorities. At the State level, the Chief Wild Life Warden exercises statutory responsibilities concerning wildlife management and specified permissions.

Specialised national institutions

InstitutionLegal basisPrincipal responsibility
National Tiger Conservation Authority (NTCA)Section 38LStatutory oversight and support for tiger conservation
Central Zoo Authority (CZA)Section 38ARecognition and regulation of zoos
Wild Life Crime Control Bureau (WCCB)Section 38YCoordination and intelligence concerning organised wildlife crime
National Board for Wild LifeSection 5ANational wildlife conservation advice and statutory functions
State Board for Wild LifeSection 6State-level wildlife conservation advice

The NTCA should not be confused with Project Tiger. Project Tiger was launched in 1973; NTCA became a statutory authority through later amendments to the Wild Life (Protection) Act.

Similarly, the WCCB addresses wildlife crime and illegal trade, whereas the CZA regulates recognised zoos. Their functions are different even though both contribute to wildlife conservation.

How responsibilities operate together

Consider illegal trade involving a protected animal. Forest and wildlife officers may investigate the offence and take action under the Act. The WCCB may assist with intelligence and coordination, especially where organised networks are involved. A State Board or the NBWL does not ordinarily replace these enforcement authorities.

For a proposed activity affecting a protected area, the applicable wildlife approval process must be followed. The existence of a State Government recommendation does not automatically establish that all national-level wildlife requirements have been met.

Prelims focus

  • NBWL: Section 5A; chaired by the Prime Minister.
  • SBWL: Section 6; chaired by the Chief Minister.
  • CZA: Section 38A; regulation and recognition of zoos.
  • NTCA: Section 38L; tiger conservation.
  • WCCB: Section 38Y; wildlife crime coordination.
  • Trap: Project Tiger, NTCA, NBWL and WCCB are distinct programmes or institutions.

[The Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972, India Code, sections 4–8, 38A–38J, 38L–38X and 38Y–38Z; National Tiger Conservation Authority, Project Tiger overview, consulted 1 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: NBWL and SBWL give conservation advice; the Warden administers state wildlife, NTCA conserves tigers, CZA regulates zoos, and WCCB addresses wildlife crime.
pictures.caption: Match each wildlife institution with its principal statutory function.

title: Wildlife Conservation Institutions and Their Responsibilities

body:
Why the 1988 policy was introduced

The National Forest Policy, 1988 was adopted through a Government of India resolution dated 7 December 1988. It followed the earlier National Forest Policy of 1952 and placed much greater emphasis on ecological stability, forest conservation and the needs of forest-dependent people.

A central change in approach was the recognition that forests should not primarily be treated as a source of government revenue. Their ecological functions are essential for soil conservation, water security, climate regulation, wildlife and the long-term well-being of society.

The principal objectives

The policy identifies the following major aims:

  • Maintain environmental stability and restore ecological balance.
  • Conserve the country's natural heritage, including biological diversity and genetic resources.
  • Check soil erosion, floods, droughts and desertification, particularly in ecologically sensitive regions.
  • Increase forest and tree cover through afforestation, social forestry and farm forestry.
  • Meet the basic needs of rural and tribal populations for fuelwood, fodder, minor forest produce and small timber, while promoting sustainable use.
  • Encourage people's participation, including the participation of women, in forest protection and management.

The one-third and two-thirds targets

One of the most frequently tested provisions appears in Section 4.1 of the policy.

The national goal is a minimum of one-third of the country's total land area under forest or tree cover. In hilly and mountainous regions, the aim is two-thirds of the area under such cover.

The higher target in mountainous regions reflects the importance of vegetation in reducing erosion, landslides and degradation of fragile ecosystems.

These are policy goals, not statements that India has already achieved those levels. They are also not the same as the legal classification of land as reserved forest or protected forest.

Community needs and sustainable forest management

The policy recognises that many communities depend on forests for their livelihoods. It calls for protection and development of minor forest produce and encourages participation in forest management.

Social forestry involves planting and managing trees to meet community needs, including on village and other suitable lands. Farm forestry involves trees grown on agricultural holdings and other privately managed land.

These approaches can reduce pressure on natural forests. However, a plantation does not automatically reproduce the biodiversity or ecological complexity of an old natural forest.

Policy and law are different

The National Forest Policy expresses governmental objectives and management priorities. By contrast, the forest conservation law imposes legally enforceable requirements for specified forest land uses. A policy target cannot itself authorise a road, mine or other project on forest land.

Prelims focus

  • National Forest Policy, 1988: resolution dated 7 December 1988.
  • Earlier National Forest Policy: 1952.
  • Section 4.1: at least one-third of total land area under forest or tree cover.
  • Hilly and mountainous regions: two-thirds forest or tree cover.
  • Environmental stability and ecological balance receive priority over a narrow revenue-oriented approach.
  • Trap: The one-third figure is a national policy target, not proof of actual forest-cover achievement.

[Government of India, National Forest Policy, 1988, resolution dated 7 December 1988, sections 2.1, 2.2, 3.1–3.5, 4.1 and 4.2; NCERT, Indian Economic Development, Class 11, Chapter 9, Environment and Sustainable Development, printed pp. 163–173. Sources consulted 1 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Forest and tree-cover targets: minimum 1/3 nationally and 2/3 in hills and mountains, where cover helps prevent soil erosion and land degradation.
pictures.caption: The policy prescribes different forest and tree-cover goals for the country and for hills.

title: National Forest Policy, 1988: Objectives, Targets and People's Participation

body:
Forest classification under the Indian Forest Act, 1927

The Indian Forest Act, 1927 provides an important legal framework for forest administration, regulation of forest produce and the classification of forests.

The central categories are:

  • Reserved forest: Land constituted as reserved forest by State Government notification under Section 20 after inquiry into and settlement of existing rights. Activities and rights are subject to relatively strict legal regulation.
  • Protected forest: Forest land notified under Section 29, subject to the Act's provisions concerning government interests, existing rights and regulated activities.
  • Village forest: Under Section 28, the State Government may assign specified rights over government forest land to a village community, subject to the legal framework.

A protected forest under the Indian Forest Act is not the same category as a wildlife sanctuary under the Wild Life (Protection) Act. Likewise, a reserved forest is not automatically a national park.

Why a separate forest conservation law was needed

Forest land can be lost even without illegal timber cutting. A government may propose to use a forest for a road, mining project, transmission facility, settlement or another non-forest activity. Such conversion can cause habitat loss and fragmentation.

To control this, Parliament enacted the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980, now officially named the Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam, 1980.

Prior approval of the Central Government

Section 2 restricts specified decisions by State Governments and other authorities unless they have obtained the prior approval of the Central Government. These include:

  • Declaring that a reserved forest, or part of one, will cease to be reserved.
  • Permitting forest land to be used for a non-forest purpose.
  • Assigning forest land by lease or otherwise to persons or organisations, subject to the statutory requirements.
  • Clearing naturally grown trees for reafforestation where the provision applies.

A State Government's ownership or management of forest land does not remove the requirement for Central Government approval under Section 2.

What counts as a non-forest purpose?

Non-forest use includes clearing forest land for activities such as mining, construction and cultivation of tea, coffee, spices, rubber, palms, oil-bearing plants, horticultural crops or medicinal plants.

The Act also identifies certain activities related to forest and wildlife conservation, development and management, such as maintaining fire lines and constructing fencing or waterholes, that are excluded from the statutory meaning of non-forest purpose, subject to the stated conditions.

The important distinction is between management of a forest as a forest and conversion of forest land to another use. The precise legal provisions determine whether approval is required.

How forest diversion approval generally works

For a proposal requiring approval, the applicant and the State authorities supply the prescribed information about the land and proposed use. The proposal is examined under the central forest clearance framework.

The approval process commonly distinguishes:

  1. In-principle or Stage-I approval: Preliminary Central Government approval subject to specified conditions.
  2. Compliance: The State Government or project proponent fulfils the applicable conditions, which may include compensatory afforestation and other safeguards.
  3. Final or Stage-II approval: Central Government approval after satisfactory compliance with the Stage-I conditions.

Compensatory afforestation seeks to replace some forest cover lost through approved diversion by establishing forests elsewhere under prescribed conditions. Net Present Value (NPV) refers to a financial assessment associated with the loss of forest ecosystem benefits. These mechanisms do not establish that ecological damage has been fully reversed.

The Compensatory Afforestation Fund Act, 2016 provides for funds and institutions relating to compensatory afforestation. It does not replace the need for approval under the forest conservation law.

A relevant procedural update

The Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Amendment Rules, 2026, notified on 11 March 2026, amended Rule 9(12). For proposals involving more than 40 hectares of forest land, the rule requires an additional field inspection by the Conservator of Forests, Chief Conservator of Forests or Regional Chief Conservator of Forests holding charge of the concerned forest circle, alongside verification by the Divisional Forest Officer. This is a procedural requirement, not a new general exemption from forest clearance.

Prelims focus

  • Indian Forest Act, 1927: reserved, protected and village forests.
  • Village forests: Section 28; protected forests: Section 29.
  • Forest conservation law: enacted in 1980 and renamed in 2023.
  • Section 2: prior Central Government approval for specified forest land decisions.
  • Stage-I means in-principle approval; Stage-II means final approval after satisfactory compliance.
  • Trap: Compensatory afforestation does not by itself authorise diversion of forest land.

[Indian Forest Act, 1927, sections 3–29; Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam, 1980, India Code, section 2; Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Rules, 2023, and Amendment Rules, 2025, rule 2; Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Amendment Rules, 2026, G.S.R. 174(E), 11 March 2026, rule 9(12); Compensatory Afforestation Fund Act, 2016. Legal texts consulted 1 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Forest diversion proceeds through examination, conditional Stage-I approval, compliance including applicable afforestation, and Stage-II final approval.
pictures.caption: Stage-I approval and final approval are distinct steps.

title: Forest Administration and the Law Regulating Diversion of Forest Land

body:
What the 2023 amendment changed

The Forest (Conservation) Amendment Act, 2023 substantially amended the 1980 law. Its main provisions took effect on 1 December 2023, when the law received its present name: Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam, 1980.

The amendment introduced Section 1A, identifying categories of land covered by the Act and specified categories excluded from its application.

Land covered under Section 1A(1)

The statutory text covers:

  • Notified forests: Land declared or notified as forest under the Indian Forest Act, 1927, or another applicable law.
  • Recorded forests: Land not covered by the first category but recorded as forest in government records on or after 25 October 1980.

The second category contains a qualification: the provision excludes land whose forest use was changed to a non-forest purpose on or before 12 December 1996 through an order of an authority authorised by the State Government or Union Territory Administration.

Government records for this purpose can include specified records held by revenue or forest departments and recognised authorities, local bodies or communities.

Specified exclusions under Section 1A(2)

The amendment provides several limited categories that are not covered by the Act, subject to the prescribed terms and conditions.

CategoryExtent or conditionImportant qualification
Access and roadside or railway amenitiesUp to 0.10 hectare in each qualifying caseApplies to the specified situations involving government-maintained roads or rail lines
Trees or plantations on land outside Section 1A(1)Specified non-covered landGrowing trees does not automatically make every parcel subject to this Act
Strategic linear projects near bordersWithin 100 km of an international border, Line of Control or Line of Actual ControlMust concern national importance and national security under the applicable conditions
Security-related infrastructureUp to 10 hectaresSubject to the applicable statutory and notified conditions
Specified projects in notified Left Wing Extremism-affected areasUp to 5 hectaresRestricted to the specified defence, paramilitary or public utility purposes

The exemption provisions are subject to Central Government conditions, including conditions concerning compensatory planting. Other applicable laws and requirements must also be considered.

The 100 km provision is not a blanket exemption for every road, railway or project within 100 km of an international border. It concerns the specified strategic linear projects of national importance and national security, subject to notified conditions.

The T. N. Godavarman forest interpretation

In T. N. Godavarman Thirumulpad v. Union of India, the Supreme Court's order of 12 December 1996 adopted a broad understanding of forest for the purpose of the forest conservation law. It recognised forests according to their dictionary meaning, statutory classifications and government records, irrespective of ownership.

The 2023 amendment's definition of covered land became the subject of constitutional litigation. In an order dated 19 February 2024, the Supreme Court directed that the earlier Godavarman principle continue to be observed pending the relevant identification exercise.

In its order dated 16 September 2026 in Ashok Kumar Sharma v. Union of India, the Supreme Court stated that the proceedings concerned the constitutional validity of the 2023 amendment. It clarified that jurisdictional High Courts may oversee forest identification where required, while the Supreme Court proceedings remain confined to the constitutional validity of the 2023 amendment.

Legal status at the content cutoff of 1 November 2026: The 2023 statutory amendment was in force, while the constitutional challenge discussed in the 16 September 2026 order had not been finally decided in that order. The statutory wording and the Court's directions must therefore be read together rather than treating the disputed scope as conclusively settled by either position.

What does not follow from the amendment?

An exclusion from this particular forest conservation law does not, by itself, abolish wildlife protection, recognised forest rights or other applicable environmental obligations. The legal consequence depends on the land, proposed activity and other laws governing that activity.

Prelims focus

  • The 2023 forest amendment took effect on 1 December 2023.
  • Section 1A(1) identifies notified and recorded forest land covered by the Act.
  • 25 October 1980 and 12 December 1996 are important dates in Section 1A.
  • Specified limits include 0.10 hectare, 100 km, 10 hectares and 5 hectares.
  • T. N. Godavarman: important Supreme Court forest interpretation dated 12 December 1996.
  • Trap: The border-related exclusion applies to qualifying strategic linear projects, not every project near a border.

[Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam, 1980, India Code, section 1A, as inserted by the Forest (Conservation) Amendment Act, 2023, effective 1 December 2023; Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change, Guidelines under Section 1A(3), S.O. 5074(E), 29 November 2023; Supreme Court of India, T. N. Godavarman Thirumulpad v. Union of India, order dated 12 December 1996, W.P.(C) 202/1995; Supreme Court of India, Ashok Kumar Sharma v. Union of India, orders dated 19 February 2024 and 16 September 2026, W.P.(C) 1164/2023. Sources consulted 1 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Section 1A(2) contrasts the conditional 100 km border-distance exclusion for strategic linear projects with area ceilings of 0.10, 10 and 5 hectares.
pictures.caption: Each statutory exclusion has its own purpose, limit and conditions.

title: The 2023 Forest Conservation Amendment: Land Coverage, Exceptions and Court Interpretation

body:
Why forest rights needed legal recognition

Many Scheduled Tribe and other traditional forest-dwelling communities have depended on forests for generations. Yet their occupation, resource use and customary rights were often not formally recorded.

The Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition of Forest Rights) Act, 2006, commonly called the Forest Rights Act (FRA), addresses this historical problem by recognising and vesting specified rights in eligible forest-dwelling communities and individuals.

The Ministry of Tribal Affairs is the nodal Union ministry for implementing the FRA.

Who is eligible?

The Act recognises 2 broad categories:

  • Forest-dwelling Scheduled Tribes: Members or communities of Scheduled Tribes who primarily reside in and depend on forests or forest land for genuine livelihood needs, subject to the Act's requirements.
  • Other Traditional Forest Dwellers (OTFDs): Persons or communities who primarily resided in and depended on forests or forest land for bona fide livelihood needs for at least 3 generations before 13 December 2005.

For this purpose, 1 generation is treated as 25 years; therefore, 3 generations means 75 years.

The date 13 December 2005 is also the important statutory cutoff concerning occupation. The FRA does not authorise new occupation of forest land after the cutoff as a way to obtain fresh rights.

Individual and community forest rights

Individual forest rights include the right of eligible people to hold and live on forest land under occupation for habitation or self-cultivation for livelihood.

The area recognised for self-cultivation is limited to land under actual occupation and cannot exceed 4 hectares under Section 4(6). This is a maximum limit, not a promise that each claimant receives 4 hectares of new land.

Rights recognised under the FRA are generally heritable but not alienable or transferable. For married persons, the Act provides for registration in the joint names of spouses.

Community rights include customary grazing, access to water bodies and fish, traditional seasonal resource access, and rights concerning minor forest produce. Minor forest produce includes resources such as bamboo, tendu leaves and honey, as covered by the statutory definition.

Community forest resource rights under Section 3(1)(i) include the authority of eligible communities to protect, regenerate, conserve or manage community forest resources traditionally protected by them.

The FRA does not grant an unrestricted right to hunt wild animals. Its recognition of forest rights must be understood alongside applicable wildlife protection law.

How claims are recognised

Under Section 6, the recognition procedure begins locally and proceeds through specified committees.

  1. Gram Sabha: Initiates the process, receives claims, verifies evidence and passes resolutions. A Forest Rights Committee assists with preparing and verifying claims.
  2. Sub-Divisional Level Committee: Examines Gram Sabha resolutions, considers objections or petitions and prepares recommendations.
  3. District Level Committee: Considers and finally approves the record of recognised forest rights. Its decision on the record is final and binding under the Act.
  4. State Level Monitoring Committee: Monitors the recognition and vesting process.

A person aggrieved by a Gram Sabha decision can petition the Sub-Divisional Level Committee within the prescribed period, ordinarily 60 days. A person aggrieved by the Sub-Divisional Level Committee's decision may petition the District Level Committee within 60 days of that decision.

Protection against eviction and relocation

Section 4(5) protects eligible forest dwellers against eviction or removal from occupied forest land until the process of recognising and verifying their rights is complete, except as otherwise provided by the Act.

For relocation from critical wildlife habitats, Section 4(2) establishes additional safeguards. They include completion of rights recognition, evidence that the activities or presence of rights holders are causing irreversible damage and threatening the species and habitat concerned, a finding that reasonable coexistence options are unavailable, and a resettlement and rehabilitation package. The process also requires the free and informed written consent of the Gram Sabhas in the areas concerned to the proposed resettlement and package; relocation must wait until the promised facilities and land allocation are complete.

Conservation and rights can reinforce one another

The FRA does not treat forest-dependent communities only as users of forest resources. It recognises that communities may also protect biodiversity, maintain customary conservation practices and manage community forest resources.

For Gujarat, this framework is especially relevant to forest-dependent communities in tribal regions, including parts of the Dangs and eastern Gujarat. Eligibility and recognition, however, are determined by the Act and evidence, not simply by residence in a particular district.

Prelims focus

  • Forest Rights Act: 2006; nodal Union ministry: Ministry of Tribal Affairs.
  • Other Traditional Forest Dwellers: 3 generations, meaning 75 years, before 13 December 2005.
  • Individual self-cultivation rights: actual occupation, maximum 4 hectares.
  • Section 3(1)(i): community forest resource conservation and management rights.
  • Section 6: Gram Sabha initiates; District Level Committee gives final approval.
  • Trap: The 4-hectare limit is not a compulsory land grant, and forest rights do not create a right to unrestricted hunting.

[Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition of Forest Rights) Act, 2006, sections 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6; Forest Rights Rules, 2008, as amended in 2012, rules 11–15; Ministry of Tribal Affairs, Forest Rights Act overview and FRA implementation portal, consulted 1 November 2026.]

title: Forest Rights Act, 2006: Individual Rights, Community Rights and Gram Sabha

body:
Why a separate biodiversity law was required

Wildlife and forest legislation can protect species, habitats and forest land. However, a different problem arises when a person or company obtains a biological resource or traditional knowledge and uses it to develop a commercial product.

For example, local communities may know how a particular plant has traditionally been used. If an outside enterprise commercially exploits that resource or associated knowledge, questions arise about lawful access and whether the knowledge holders should share in the resulting benefits.

The Biological Diversity Act, 2002 provides a legal framework for these matters. The Act received presidential assent on 5 February 2003. Its administrative provisions began operating on 1 October 2003, while provisions relating to access and benefit sharing began operating on 1 July 2004.

The three objectives

The Act implements India's commitments under the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD), opened for signature at the Rio Earth Summit in 1992.

Its 3 principal objectives are:

  1. Conservation of biological diversity: Protecting genetic, species and ecosystem diversity.
  2. Sustainable use: Using biological resources without undermining their continued availability and ecological functions.
  3. Fair and equitable benefit sharing: Ensuring appropriate sharing of benefits arising from the use of biological resources and associated traditional knowledge.

The third objective is particularly distinctive. Biodiversity law is not limited to protecting an animal or planting trees; it also concerns fairness in the utilisation of biological resources.

Three-tier institutional structure

The Act establishes a decentralised system of national, State and local institutions.

LevelInstitutionPrincipal role
NationalNational Biodiversity Authority (NBA)National regulation, approvals, advice and benefit-sharing functions
StateState Biodiversity Board (SBB)State advice and regulation of specified access and commercial use
LocalBiodiversity Management Committee (BMC)Documentation, conservation and participation in local biodiversity management

The National Biodiversity Authority is established under Section 8 and is headquartered in Chennai. State Biodiversity Boards operate under Section 22. Biodiversity Management Committees are provided for under Section 41.

In Union Territories, the relevant statutory arrangements include Union Territory Biodiversity Councils.

Biodiversity Management Committees

A BMC works at the local-body level, including Gram Panchayats in rural areas and relevant municipal bodies in urban areas.

Its functions include documenting and supporting conservation of local biodiversity, habitats, cultivated varieties, domesticated breeds and associated traditional knowledge.

Under the amended Act, a BMC has not fewer than 7 and not more than 11 members, with its composition determined under the applicable State framework.

People's Biodiversity Register

The People's Biodiversity Register (PBR) is a local record prepared through the BMC framework. It documents biological resources and associated knowledge within the local jurisdiction.

A PBR may record local plants and animals, crop varieties, useful biological resources, conservation practices and traditional knowledge. The information helps communities and authorities understand local biodiversity and identify resources needing conservation.

BMC means the local committee. PBR means the register of biodiversity information prepared through that framework. The committee and the register are not interchangeable.

A PBR is not itself a forest land title, a wildlife trade licence or a general commercial access permit. Separate legal provisions govern those matters.

Biodiversity Heritage Sites

Section 37 provides for the declaration of Biodiversity Heritage Sites (BHSs) by the State Government on the recommendation of the State Biodiversity Board, which must first consult the local body and the BMC concerned.

Such sites recognise areas of biodiversity importance and conservation value. They must not be confused with national parks declared under the Wild Life (Protection) Act.

Gujarat connection

Gujarat implements the national biodiversity framework through its State biodiversity institutions and local BMCs. The Gujarat Biological Diversity Rules, 2010 provide an important State-level regulatory reference.

Local biodiversity documentation is relevant to Gujarat's varied habitats, including the Gir landscape, coastal ecosystems, dry grasslands and tribal forest regions. The BMC and PBR framework can record local biodiversity even where the area is not designated as a national park or wildlife sanctuary.

Prelims focus

  • Biological Diversity Act, 2002: conservation, sustainable use and equitable benefit sharing.
  • CBD: opened for signature at Rio in 1992.
  • NBA: Section 8; headquarters at Chennai.
  • SBB: Section 22; BMC: Section 41.
  • PBR: People's Biodiversity Register, prepared through the local biodiversity framework.
  • Trap: A BMC is an institution; a PBR is a record. Neither is a national park declaration.

[Biological Diversity Act, 2002, as amended, sections 8, 22, 37 and 41; National Biodiversity Authority, Frequently Asked Questions, questions 1–5 and 11–14, consulted 1 November 2026; National Biodiversity Authority, State Biodiversity Rules directory, Gujarat Biological Diversity Rules, 2010, consulted 1 November 2026; Convention on Biological Diversity, 1992, Articles 1 and 15.]

pictures.alt: NBA, SBB and BMC form the national, State and local institutions; BMC prepares the People's Biodiversity Register, a local record.
pictures.caption: Biodiversity governance connects national regulation with State and local institutions.

title: Biological Diversity Act, 2002: Objectives, Institutions and People's Biodiversity Registers

body:
Meaning of access and benefit sharing

Access and Benefit Sharing (ABS) governs the relationship between persons using biological resources or associated traditional knowledge and those entitled to a fair share of benefits arising from their utilisation.

Access can involve obtaining biological resources or associated knowledge for purposes covered by the Act. Benefit sharing concerns the fair distribution of resulting benefits, especially to relevant communities or knowledge holders.

Benefits need not always be cash payments. Depending on the applicable agreement and legal framework, they may include monetary payments, technology transfer, research participation, capacity building or support for conservation.

Who regulates access?

The Biological Diversity Act distinguishes different users and activities. A useful preliminary distinction is between persons covered by Section 3(2) and persons covered by Section 7.

User categoryResearch or bio-surveyCommercial utilisation
Section 3(2) personPrior NBA approval required for regulated accessPrior NBA approval required
Section 7 personGenerally no NBA or SBB access approval required for qualifying Indian researchPrior intimation and approval through the concerned SBB or applicable UT authority, subject to exemptions

Section 3(2) persons include foreign citizens, Indian citizens who are non-residents as defined by the Act, and specified foreign entities or Indian-registered entities controlled by foreigners. An Indian-registered company's status must therefore be assessed under the amended legal definition; registration in India alone does not settle the question. Foreign control includes the right to appoint a majority of directors or to control management or policy decisions, directly or indirectly.

Section 7 persons generally include Indian persons and entities not falling within Section 3(2), subject to the statutory definitions and exceptions.

Separate requirements apply to certain intellectual property rights, commercialisation of intellectual property and transfers of research results. For example, Section 7 applicants must register with the NBA and Section 3(2) applicants must obtain NBA approval before the IPR is granted; NBA approval is also required for commercialisation.

How communities participate

Benefit sharing is not simply a payment to the Central Government. The purpose includes ensuring that relevant benefit claimers, including local communities and holders of associated traditional knowledge, receive appropriate benefits.

The NBA or SBB follows the prescribed consultation process involving the relevant BMCs and communities when examining regulated access requests. Prior informed consent means that the concerned providers or knowledge holders are appropriately informed before consenting under the applicable process. Mutually agreed terms describe the negotiated conditions governing access and benefit sharing.

Illustrative application

Suppose an enterprise seeks to develop a commercial product using a biological resource and associated knowledge obtained from a village. The relevant authority first determines the user category and applicable regulatory requirements. The resource and knowledge holders are considered through the statutory consultation process. If the activity is regulated, approval and benefit-sharing conditions are determined under the applicable law.

The enterprise cannot assume that knowledge obtained from a public discussion is automatically free from biodiversity-law obligations.

Important exemptions and qualifications

Section 7 contains exemptions for specified categories, including certain local community activities, codified traditional knowledge (knowledge derived from authoritative books specified in the First Schedule to the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940), cultivated medicinal plants and their products, and eligible traditional practitioners, subject to the amended legal conditions.

The exemption for commercial utilisation of cultivated medicinal plants under the applicable amended rules requires a Certificate of Origin from the relevant BMC. It is therefore inaccurate to say that every medicinal plant transaction is automatically exempt from all biodiversity regulation.

Also, an exemption relating to codified traditional knowledge must not be confused with an unrestricted exemption for accessing the biological resource itself. The status of the resource, user and activity must be examined separately.

The National Biodiversity Authority and State Biodiversity Boards have different approval responsibilities. Prior NBA approval is not the universal requirement for every Indian researcher or every commercial user.

Prelims focus

  • ABS means Access and Benefit Sharing.
  • Section 3: specified foreign and foreign-controlled categories; NBA regulates relevant access.
  • Section 7: specified Indian-category persons; SBB regulates qualifying commercial utilisation.
  • BMCs participate in community consultation and local benefit-sharing processes.
  • Benefits can be monetary or non-monetary.
  • Trap: Indian research, Indian commercial utilisation and access by a foreign-controlled entity do not automatically follow identical approval requirements.

[Biological Diversity Act, 2002, as amended by Act 10 of 2023, sections 2–7, 19–24, 41 and related provisions; National Biodiversity Authority, Frequently Asked Questions, questions 17, 20–25 and 29–32; National Biodiversity Authority, Biological Diversity Rules, 2024, and Biological Diversity (Amendment) Rules, 2025, including rule 19. Official sources consulted 1 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Section 3(2) users need NBA prior approval; Section 7 commercial use is regulated by SBB. BMC consultation connects to local participation and benefit sharing.
pictures.caption: Regulated access connects biological resource users with local benefit claimers.

title: Access and Benefit Sharing: Who Needs Approval and Who Receives Benefits?

body:
Why the 2023 amendment matters

The Biological Diversity (Amendment) Act, 2023 changed several important features of India's biodiversity regulation. It came into force on 1 April 2024.

The amendment sought to simplify certain procedures while retaining the Act's main objectives: conservation, sustainable use and equitable benefit sharing. It also addressed aspects of the Nagoya Protocol, adopted in 2010 under the Convention on Biological Diversity.

Major changes for prelims

  • Regulatory simplification: Procedures for certain access, research, commercial activities and intellectual property matters were revised.
  • Medicinal plants and traditional knowledge: Specified exemptions were introduced or clarified, particularly for cultivated medicinal plants, eligible traditional practitioners and codified traditional knowledge.
  • State-level powers: The regulatory role of State Biodiversity Boards was clarified and strengthened.
  • Local governance: Biodiversity Management Committees received strengthened statutory recognition, including provisions concerning composition and certificates of origin for cultivated medicinal plants.
  • Penalties: Certain offences were decriminalised by replacing imprisonment provisions with monetary penalties and an adjudication mechanism.

Decriminalisation does not mean an activity has become lawful or that all penalties have disappeared. It means the legal consequences and enforcement mechanism for specified violations have changed.

The 2024 and 2025 rules

The Biological Diversity Rules, 2024 were notified on 22 October 2024 and came into force on 21 December 2024, replacing the earlier 2004 rules.

The Biological Diversity (Amendment) Rules, 2025 were notified on 6 May 2025 and came into force on 1 November 2025. They included provisions concerning the BMC's Certificate of Origin for cultivated medicinal plants.

The Biological Diversity (Access to Biological Resources and Knowledge Associated Thereto and Fair and Equitable Sharing of Benefits) Regulations, 2025 provide the detailed regulatory framework for relevant access and benefit-sharing matters.

What remains unchanged in principle?

Despite procedural changes, the legislation continues to link conservation with sustainable utilisation and fairness to communities and knowledge holders.

The amended framework also preserves distinctions between national and State responsibilities. A foreign-controlled entity cannot automatically rely on an exemption intended for qualifying Indian-category persons. Similarly, an Indian commercial user must consider the applicable SBB requirements even where the activity does not require the same approval as a foreign-category user.

Legal status at the selected cutoff

As at the 1 November 2026 content cutoff, the 2023 amendment was in force, the 2024 rules had commenced, and the 2025 amendment rules had also commenced. The original 2002 Act must therefore be studied together with these amendments and subordinate rules.

Older summaries describing only the unamended 2002 Act may give incorrect answers about user categories, approval requirements, BMC composition or penalties.

Prelims focus

  • Biological Diversity (Amendment) Act, 2023: effective 1 April 2024.
  • Biological Diversity Rules, 2024: effective 21 December 2024.
  • Biological Diversity (Amendment) Rules, 2025: effective 1 November 2025.
  • Nagoya Protocol: adopted in 2010.
  • Amended BMC membership: 7 to 11 members.
  • Trap: Replacing imprisonment with monetary penalties for specified violations does not eliminate regulatory obligations.

[Biological Diversity (Amendment) Act, 2023, Act 10 of 2023; Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change, commencement notification S.O. 295(E), 18 January 2024; Biological Diversity Rules, 2024, notified 22 October 2024; Biological Diversity (Amendment) Rules, 2025, notified 6 May 2025; National Biodiversity Authority, Frequently Asked Questions, questions 6, 7, 10 and 14; National Biodiversity Authority, Access and Benefit Sharing regulatory information, consulted 1 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Timeline separates the 2002 Act’s assent and phased commencement from the commencement dates of the 2023 amendment and later rules.
pictures.caption: The amendment, commencement dates and later rules are different legal events.

title: Biological Diversity Amendments and the Current Legal Framework

body:
One activity may be governed by several laws

Indian environmental laws should not be understood as isolated alternatives. The same land or resource may be governed by different laws for different reasons.

Consider a hypothetical proposal to construct infrastructure through forest land in Gujarat near a wildlife habitat used by a protected species and by a forest-dependent village community.

Several separate questions arise:

  1. Forest land: Is the land covered by the Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam, 1980? If so, does the proposed activity require prior Central Government approval under Section 2?
  2. Wildlife: Does the land lie within a national park, wildlife sanctuary, tiger reserve or another regulated area? Are protected species or their habitats affected? Applicable requirements under the Wild Life (Protection) Act must be considered.
  3. Forest rights: Are there eligible individual or community rights under the Forest Rights Act, 2006? Have the prescribed processes and safeguards concerning those rights been followed?
  4. Biological resources: Does any separate activity involve regulated access to biological resources or associated traditional knowledge? If so, the Biological Diversity Act may impose additional requirements.

Receiving forest diversion approval does not automatically settle the questions arising under wildlife law, forest-rights law or biodiversity law. Similarly, recognition of a forest right does not by itself grant permission to hunt a protected animal.

How to distinguish the institutions

Each authority should be identified by the legal question it answers.

  • Central Government under the forest conservation law: Prior approval for specified forest land decisions.
  • NBWL and SBWL: Wildlife conservation advice and prescribed wildlife-related functions.
  • Chief Wild Life Warden: State-level statutory wildlife administration and specified permissions.
  • Gram Sabha and District Level Committee: Beginning and final institutional stages of forest-rights recognition.
  • NBA and SBB: Regulation of specified biological resource access and benefit sharing.
  • BMC: Local biodiversity documentation, conservation and community participation.

Five distinctions that prevent common errors

First: A reserved forest is a forest-administration classification; a national park is a wildlife protected-area designation.

Second: Forest or tree-cover targets under the National Forest Policy are policy goals; they are not the same as statutory forest land classifications or clearance requirements.

Third: Recognition of individual and community forest rights under the FRA is different from a commercial licence to exploit forest products without regulation.

Fourth: The Wildlife Act's legal schedules are distinct from scientific conservation classifications such as the IUCN Red List.

Fifth: A People's Biodiversity Register documents local biodiversity; it is not equivalent to a national or State approval for commercial access.

Integrated revision picture

When a prelims question mentions a road or mining project on forest land, begin with the forest diversion law. When it mentions hunting or a legally protected animal, begin with the Wild Life (Protection) Act. When it concerns customary forest occupation, minor forest produce or community forest management, begin with the Forest Rights Act. When it concerns commercial use of biological resources, traditional knowledge or benefit sharing, begin with the Biological Diversity Act.

Prelims focus

  • Wildlife protection: Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972.
  • Forest diversion: Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam, 1980.
  • Forest policy targets: National Forest Policy, 1988.
  • Recognised individual and community forest rights: Forest Rights Act, 2006.
  • Biological resource access and benefit sharing: Biological Diversity Act, 2002.
  • Trap: Approval under one environmental law does not automatically replace the requirements of another applicable law.

[The Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972, sections 9, 18–36D and 38V; Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam, 1980, sections 1A and 2; National Forest Policy, 1988, sections 2–4; Forest Rights Act, 2006, sections 3, 4 and 6; Biological Diversity Act, 2002, as amended, sections 3, 7, 8, 22 and 41; National Biodiversity Authority, Frequently Asked Questions, questions 8 and 9. Sources consulted 1 November 2026.]
